claims.text: Corrosion resistance in both chemical-processing and nuclear-power steels is primarily governed by a uniform, stoichiometric, Cr-rich passive oxide layer.
Electrochemical surface pre-treatment enhances formation and adherence of the protective Cr-rich layer on austenitic stainless steel.
An optimized Cr:Mo ratio in Fe-Cr-Mo steel promotes a robust, self-healing passive film under high-temperature and high-pressure conditions.
Quantifying roughness while electrochemically polishing the samples can decouple topographical effects from oxide chemistry.
High-pressure water at approximately 300 degrees Celsius represents nuclear-coolant exposure conditions relevant to the proposed steel tests.
The governing structural mediator is a coherent, continuous, stoichiometric Cr2O3-rich film that is compositionally uniform and free of localized defects.
Electrochemical polishing improves surface finish and minimizes microstructural defects.
The improved surface finish produced by electrochemical polishing promotes uniform oxide formation.
A favorable Cr:Mo ratio intrinsically improves the ability of Fe-Cr-Mo steel to form and maintain a stable, self-healing Cr-rich film.
A compact, self-healing Cr2O3 layer acts as a diffusion barrier against further oxidation.
Greater chromium enrichment of stainless-steel passive films is associated with improved corrosion resistance.
Electrochemically polished austenitic stainless steel will have a lower corrosion rate than untreated steel in the specified ambient acid or chloride media.
Electrochemically polished samples will form more uniform and adherent Cr-rich oxide layers than untreated samples.
Electrochemically polished samples will have fewer initiation sites for localized corrosion.
Fe-Cr-Mo alloys with optimized Cr:Mo ratios will show steadier oxide growth, lower corrosion rates, and higher electrochemical stability than baseline compositions under autoclave conditions.
Mechanical damage, extreme thermal stress, or uncontrolled microstructural variation may place the proposed mechanism outside its applicable boundary.
Secondary-phase formation and other microstructural artifacts can confound the inferred effect of the Cr:Mo ratio.
Failure of either intervention to improve film properties or corrosion rate would falsify the claim that a uniform Cr-rich passive film governs corrosion resistance.
